full_judgment:
It may be pointed out here that in the present case the respondent was set at liberty after the order of acquittal was passed as no intimation was given to the Trial Court that an appeal was going to be filed by the Government. The respondents are not therefore in custody but the learned Deputy Attorney-General argues that the appeal having been admitted by this Court against the order of acquittal, the respondents are accused in the eye of law and should be arrested as provided u/s. 427 of the Code. He further submits that after the arrest of the accused (respondent) they cannot be enlarged on bail though the power to admit them to bail has been provided in section 427 of the Code. His contention is that the provisions of section 427 to grant bail to an accused after his arrest is inconsistent with the provisions of the Order and consequently this provision providing the power to grant bail being inconsistent with the Order shall not be applicable. We are unable to accept this contention of the learned Deputy Attorney General as we find that the Order is silent about the procedure to be followed after an appeal against an order of acquittal is presented before the High Court. 

 4. We have heard Mr. Abdul Hye Choudhury, the learned Advocate as an amicus curiae. He has argued that Article 14 of the Order is not attracted to an appeal against an order of acquittal. This Article is applicable up to the trial stage of the case. He has pointed out that the procedure to be followed, when the Government desires to present an appeal to the High Court from an order of acquittal, has been laid down under Sub-Article (2) of Article 16 of the Order, which provides that the Government may direct the Public Prosecutor to present an appeal to the High Court from an order of acquittal passed by a Special Tribunal or a Special Magistrate; upon intimation to the Special Tribunal or to the Special Magistrate by the Public Prosecutor, that an appeal is being filed, the person in respect of whom the order of acquittal was passed shall continue to remain in custody. Sub-Article (2) of Article 16 empowers the Special Tribunal or the Special Magistrate to direct that the person in respect of whom the order of acquittal is passed shall continue to remain in custody upon such intimation by the Public Prosecutor that an appeal is being filed. Sub-Article (2) does not, however, specify the period of detention in custody on intimation by the Public Prosecutor regarding the fact that an appeal is being filed. Sub-Article (3) provides 60 days from the date of an appeal against an order of acquittal. It is, therefore, evident that the person who is acquitted can be kept in custody at best for a period of 60 days to enable the Government for filing an appeal within 60 days from the date of an order of acquittal. If no appeal is filed within the prescribed period the person in respect of whom the order of acquittal is passed cannot be kept in custody after the said period of 60 days. Here a pertinent question arises whether the acquitted person shall continue to remain in custody if the appeal is filed within the prescribed period. The learned Deputy Attorney General contends that the said person shall continue to remain in custody till the disposal of the appeal. Here again we find it difficult to accept the contention of the learned Deputy Attorney General. The Order seems to be silent in this respect. It may be pointed out that the order does not contain any provisions as to how a person in respect of whom an order of acquittal is passed and set at liberty, there being no intimation to the Tribunal or the Special Magistrate that an appeal is going to be filed, is to be dealt with, if subsequently Government desires to file an appeal against the said Order of acquittal. The Order does not contain any provision similar to those of section 427 of the Code, that the said person may be arrested and committed to prison pending the disposal of the appeal. Consequently, the learned Deputy Attorney General has invoked the aid of section 427 of the Code. But he has tried to bifurcate the provisions of section 427 of the Code saying that the part of the said section which is not inconsistent with the Order will apply but the part which is inconsistent will not apply. In other words, his contention is that a warrant directing the arrest of the respondent should be issued and he be taken into custody and shall not be admitted to bail pending the disposal of the appeal. It is strange to hear the learned Deputy Attorney General make his submission as above. According to his arguments, whatever is favorable for the prosecution should be done without giving any consideration to the accused despite an order of acquittal in his favour. We are constrained to hold that the submission made by the learned Deputy Attorney General does not get support either from the provisions of the Order itself or from the provisions of section 427 of the Code. It is also to be noted here that Article 16(2) only enables the Government to prefer an appeal against an order of acquittal. It does not indicate anything about the procedure to be followed in enter1aining the appeal, Obviously, the legislature did not think it name to indicate about the procedure to be following, because, by allowing the right of appeal, the proceeding before the Special Tribunal or the Special" Magistrate, has been made amenable to the criminal appellate jurisdiction of the High Court. This appellate jurisdiction is to be exercised according to the procedure laid down in the Code of Criminal Procedure. In view of the enabling provision in Article 16(2) of the Order, an appeal is to be preferred in accordance with the procedure as provided in the Code. In the instant case the appeal has been filed under Article 16(2) of the Order read with section 417 of the Code. In dealing with such appeals the High Court will exercise its criminal appellate jurisdiction as laid down in the Code. We are of the view that the provisions of section 427 of the Code are to be availed of as a whole, that is to say, that when an appeal is presented, the High Court may issue a warrant directing that the accused be arrested and committed to prison or admitted to bail. It is the discretion of the High Court either to issue warrant or not to issue warrant for the arrest of the accused when an appeal is presented before the Court against an order of acquittal. It is, therefore, evident that in appropriate cases this Court may issue warrant for the arrest of the accused and commit him to prison pending the disposal of the appeal. But this discretionary power should not necessarily be used in all eases as soon as an appeal is preferred. In this connection Mr. Abdul Hype Choudhury has referred to a passage of Interpretation of Statutes by Maxwell, 11th Edition page 274 which runs as follows:— 

 "The tendency of modern decisions, upon the whole is to narrow materially the difference between what is called a strict and a beneficial construction. All statutes are now construed with a more attentive regards to the language, and criminal statutes with a more rational regards to the aim and intention of the legislature, than formerly. It is unquestionably right that the distinction should not be altogether erased from the judicial mind, for it is required by the spirit of our free institutions that the interpretation of all statutes should be favorable to personal liberty, and this tendency is still evidenced in a certain reluctance to supply the defects of language, or to take out the meaning of an obscure passage by strained or doubtful influences. The effect of the rule of strict construction might almost be summed up in the remark that, where an equivocal word or ambiguous sentence leaves a reasonable, doubt of its meaning which the canons of interpretation fail to solve, the benefit of, the doubt should be given to the subject and against the legislature which has failed to explain itself. But it yields to the paramount rule that every statute is to be expounded according to its expressed or manifest intention and that all cases within the mischiefs aimed at are, if the language permits, to be held to fall within its remedial influence." 

 5. In view of the fact that after the order of acquittal was passed in this case it was not represented to the Tribunal by the Public Prosecutor for keeping the acquitted person in custody on the ground that the Government would file an appeal, the Tribunal directed the immediate release of the respondents. We do not, therefore, think it proper to, pass an order for arrest of the respondents.
